items.title: Introduction

sections.normalized_html: A set of Boolean functions (logical operations) is functionally complete if any Boolean function can be expressed in terms of the functions (operations) from this set.
sections.readable_text: A set of Boolean functions (logical operations) is functionally complete if any Boolean function can be expressed in terms of the functions (operations) from this set.

sections.normalized_html: For example, the set [MATH: \big\{\lnot,\: \land\big\}] containing negation and conjunction is functionally complete. To prove this, we show that we can represent any arbitrary Boolean function using only [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \land,] as follows:
sections.readable_text:
For example, the set
[MATH: \big\{\lnot,\: \land\big\}]
containing negation and conjunction is functionally complete. To prove this, we show that we can represent any arbitrary Boolean function using only [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \land,] as follows:

sections.normalized_html:
Any Boolean function can be expressed in disjunctive normal form (DNF), i.e., as an expression consisting of variables and the operators [MATH: \lor, \land,] and [MATH: \lnot] only.

In this expression, we can keep [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \land,] but replace any occurrence of a conjunction [MATH: \lor] using De Morgan's law for disjunction: [MATH: \lnot\left(A \lor B\right) \equiv \lnot A \land \lnot B] The resulting expression uses only [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \land.] Therefore, any Boolean function can be expressed in terms of [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \land,]; hence, the set [MATH: \{\lnot, \land\}] is functionally complete.

items.readable_text:
Content:
A set of Boolean functions (logical operations) is functionally complete if any Boolean function can be expressed in terms of the functions (operations) from this set.

Content:
For example, the set
[MATH: \big\{\lnot,\: \land\big\}]
containing negation and conjunction is functionally complete. To prove this, we show that we can represent any arbitrary Boolean function using only [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \land,] as follows:

Content:
> Any Boolean function can be expressed in disjunctive normal form (DNF), i.e., as an expression consisting of variables and the operators [MATH: \lor, \land,] and [MATH: \lnot] only.
>
> In this expression, we can keep [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \land,] but replace any occurrence of a conjunction [MATH: \lor] using De Morgan's law for disjunction:
> [MATH: \lnot\left(A \lor B\right) \equiv \lnot A \land \lnot B]
> The resulting expression uses only [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \land.] Therefore, any Boolean function can be expressed in terms of [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \land,]; hence, the set [MATH: \{\lnot, \land\}] is functionally complete.

Content:
Let's express [MATH: x \lor \left(y \land z\right)] using only [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \land.]
First, we use the double negation rule, [MATH: A \equiv \lnot \lnot A{:}]
[MATH: x \lor \left(y \land z\right) \equiv \lnot\lnot\big(x \lor \left(y \land z\right)\big)]

Content:
Next, we use De Morgan's law for disjunction, [MATH: \lnot (A \lor B) \equiv \lnot A \land\lnot B.]
Substituting [MATH: x] for [MATH: A] and [MATH: \left(y \land z\right)] for [MATH: B,] we get
[MATH: \lnot\lnot\big(x \lor \left(y \land z\right)\big) \equiv \lnot \left(\lnot x \land \lnot \left(y \land z\right) \right).]

Content:
Therefore, expressed using only [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \land,] we have
[MATH: x \lor \left(y \land z\right) \equiv \lnot \left(\lnot x \land \lnot \left(y \land z\right) \right)]

Content:
By similar reasoning, we can prove that the set containing negation and conjunction
[MATH: \big\{\lnot, \lor\big\}]
is also functionally complete. Let's see how to express a function using only the operations from this set in the following example.

items.title: Peirce Arrow

sections.normalized_html: The set [MATH: \{\downarrow\}] (Peirce arrow) is functionally complete. Here's the proof:
sections.readable_text: The set [MATH: \{\downarrow\}] (Peirce arrow) is functionally complete. Here's the proof:

sections.normalized_html:
Since [MATH: \{\lnot, \lor\}] is a functionally complete set, any Boolean function can be expressed in terms of only [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \lor.]

In this expression, we can replace any occurrence of disjunction [MATH: \lor] using the definition of Peirce arrow: [MATH: A \downarrow B \equiv \lnot \left(A \lor B \right)] Then, we can replace any occurrence of negation [MATH: \lnot] using the definition of the Peirce arrow for two identical variables: [MATH: A↓A|≡¬(A∨A); ≡¬A] The resulting expression uses only [MATH: \downarrow.] Therefore, any Boolean function can be expressed in terms of [MATH: \downarrow,] and hence, the set [MATH: \{\downarrow\}] is functionally complete.

>

> [MATH: A↓A|≡¬(A∨A); ≡¬A]
> The resulting expression uses only [MATH: \downarrow.] Therefore, any Boolean function can be expressed in terms of [MATH: \downarrow,] and hence, the set [MATH: \{\downarrow\}] is functionally complete.

Content:
A functionally complete set of Boolean functions is minimal if it has no functionally complete proper subset.
In other words, removing any single element results in a no longer functionally complete set.

Content:
For example, [MATH: \{\lnot, \land\}] is a minimal functionally complete set. If we remove [MATH: \land,] then the Boolean function [MATH: f \equiv x \land y] cannot be expressed using only [MATH: \lnot.]

Content:
On the other hand, [MATH: \{\lnot, \land, \lor\}] is not a minimal functionally complete set. It has proper subsets that are also functionally complete, namely [MATH: \{\lnot, \land\}] and [MATH: \{\lnot, \lor\}.]

- Negation and Disjunction: [MATH: \{\lnot, \lor\}]
- Negation and Implication (or Converse Implication): [MATH: \{\lnot, \Rightarrow\}] or [MATH: \{\lnot, \Leftarrow\}]
- Exclusive OR and Implication (or Converse Implication): [MATH: \{\oplus, \Rightarrow\}] or [MATH: \{\oplus, \Leftarrow\}]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A set of Boolean functions (logical operations) is functionally complete if any Boolean function can be expressed in terms of the functions (operations) from this set.

Content:
For example, the set
[MATH: \big\{\lnot,\: \land\big\}]
containing negation and conjunction is functionally complete. To prove this, we show that we can represent any arbitrary Boolean function using only [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \land,] as follows:

Content:
> Any Boolean function can be expressed in disjunctive normal form (DNF), i.e., as an expression consisting of variables and the operators [MATH: \lor, \land,] and [MATH: \lnot] only.
>
> In this expression, we can keep [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \land,] but replace any occurrence of a conjunction [MATH: \lor] using De Morgan's law for disjunction:
> [MATH: \lnot\left(A \lor B\right) \equiv \lnot A \land \lnot B]
> The resulting expression uses only [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \land.] Therefore, any Boolean function can be expressed in terms of [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \land,]; hence, the set [MATH: \{\lnot, \land\}] is functionally complete.

Content:
Let's express [MATH: x \lor \left(y \land z\right)] using only [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \land.]
First, we use the double negation rule, [MATH: A \equiv \lnot \lnot A{:}]
[MATH: x \lor \left(y \land z\right) \equiv \lnot\lnot\big(x \lor \left(y \land z\right)\big)]

Content:
Next, we use De Morgan's law for disjunction, [MATH: \lnot (A \lor B) \equiv \lnot A \land\lnot B.]
Substituting [MATH: x] for [MATH: A] and [MATH: \left(y \land z\right)] for [MATH: B,] we get
[MATH: \lnot\lnot\big(x \lor \left(y \land z\right)\big) \equiv \lnot \left(\lnot x \land \lnot \left(y \land z\right) \right).]

Content:
Therefore, expressed using only [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \land,] we have
[MATH: x \lor \left(y \land z\right) \equiv \lnot \left(\lnot x \land \lnot \left(y \land z\right) \right)]

Content:
By similar reasoning, we can prove that the set containing negation and conjunction
[MATH: \big\{\lnot, \lor\big\}]
is also functionally complete. Let's see how to express a function using only the operations from this set in the following example.

---

Item 2 — Example: Expressing Boolean Functions Using Negation, Conjunction, and Disjunction

Example Prompt:
Express [MATH: x \land y] (conjunction) using only [MATH: \lnot] (negation) and [MATH: \lor] (disjunction).

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we use the double negation rule, [MATH: A \equiv \lnot \lnot A{:}]

[MATH: x∧y|≡¬¬(x∧y)]

Next, we use De Morgan's law for conjunction, [MATH: \lnot (A \land B) \equiv \lnot A \lor\lnot B{:}]

[MATH: ¬¬(x∧y)|≡¬(¬x∨¬y)]

---

Item 3 — Question 1

Prompt:
Express [MATH: x⇒y] (implication) using only [MATH: ¬] (negation) and [MATH: ∧] (conjunction).

Choices:
a. [MATH: ¬(¬x∧y)]
b. [MATH: ¬(x∧y)]
c. [MATH: ¬(x∧¬y)]
d. [MATH: ¬x∧¬y]
e. [MATH: ¬(¬x∧¬y)]

---

b. [MATH: x∨¬y]
c. [MATH: ¬(x∨y)]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Negation and Implication

Content:
The set containing negation and implication
[MATH: \big\{\lnot,\: \Rightarrow\big\}]
is a functionally complete. We can prove this as follows:

Content:
> Since [MATH: \{\lnot, \lor\}] is a functionally complete set, any Boolean function can be expressed in terms of only [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \lor.]
>
> In this expression, we can keep [MATH: \lnot], but replace any occurrence of a disjunction [MATH: \lor] using the fact that
> [MATH: \lnot A \lor B \equiv A \Rightarrow B.]
> The resulting expression uses only [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \Rightarrow.] Therefore, any Boolean function can be expressed in terms of [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \Rightarrow,] and hence, the set [MATH: \{\lnot, \Rightarrow\}] is functionally complete.

Content:
Let's express [MATH: x \lor (y \land z)] using only [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \Rightarrow.]

Content:
First, we write the expression in terms of [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \lor.] Using the double negation rule [MATH: A \equiv \lnot \lnot A,] we have
[MATH: x \lor (y \land z)
\equiv x \lor \lnot\lnot(y \land z).]

Content:
Then, we apply De Morgan's law for conjunction, [MATH: \lnot (A \land B) \equiv \lnot A \lor\lnot B{:}]
[MATH: x \lor \lnot\lnot(y \land z) \equiv x \lor \lnot\left(\lnot y \lor \lnot z\right)]

Content:
Now, we write the expression in terms of [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \Rightarrow.] Using the commutativity of disjunction, [MATH: A\lor B\equiv B\lor A,] followed by the definition of implication [MATH: A \Rightarrow B \equiv \lnot A \lor B,] we get
[MATH: x∨¬(¬y∨¬z)|≡¬(¬y∨¬z)∨x; ≡(¬y∨¬z)⇒x; ≡(y⇒¬z)⇒x.]

Content:
Therefore, expressed using only [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \Rightarrow,] we have
[MATH: x \lor y \land z \equiv \left(y \Rightarrow \lnot z\right) \Rightarrow x.]

---

Item 6 — Example: Expressing Boolean Functions Using Negation and Implication

Example Prompt:
Express [MATH: x \lor y \lor z] using only [MATH: \lnot] (negation) and [MATH: \Rightarrow] (implication).

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we need to get the expression for [MATH: \lor] using only [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \Rightarrow.]

In the definition of implication [MATH: A \Rightarrow B \equiv \lnot A \lor B,] substitute [MATH: \lnot C] for [MATH: A] to get the following equivalence:

[MATH: ¬C⇒B|≡C∨B, or; C∨B|≡¬C⇒B]

Now, using the equivalence above, we substitute the expression for the first and second [MATH: \lor] in the given expression:

[MATH: x∨y∨z|≡x∨(y∨z); ≡¬x⇒(y∨z); ≡¬x⇒(¬y⇒z)]

---

b. [MATH: (x⇒¬y)⇒¬z]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Peirce Arrow

Content:
The set [MATH: \{\downarrow\}] (Peirce arrow) is functionally complete. Here's the proof:

Content:
> Since [MATH: \{\lnot, \lor\}] is a functionally complete set, any Boolean function can be expressed in terms of only [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \lor.]
>
> In this expression, we can replace any occurrence of disjunction [MATH: \lor] using the definition of Peirce arrow:
> [MATH: A \downarrow B \equiv \lnot \left(A \lor B \right)]
> Then, we can replace any occurrence of negation [MATH: \lnot] using the definition of the Peirce arrow for two identical variables:
> [MATH: A↓A|≡¬(A∨A); ≡¬A]
> The resulting expression uses only [MATH: \downarrow.] Therefore, any Boolean function can be expressed in terms of [MATH: \downarrow,] and hence, the set [MATH: \{\downarrow\}] is functionally complete.

Content:
Let's express [MATH: x \land \lnot y] using only [MATH: \downarrow.]

Content:
First, we write the expression in terms of [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \lor.] Using the double negation rule [MATH: A \equiv \lnot\lnot A,] we have
[MATH: x \land \lnot y
\equiv
\lnot\lnot (x \land \lnot y).]

Content:
Then, we apply De Morgan's law for conjunction, [MATH: \lnot(A \land B) \equiv \lnot A \lor \lnot B,] followed by the double negation rule:
[MATH: ¬¬(x∧¬y)≡¬(¬x∨¬¬y); ≡¬(¬x∨y)]

Content:
Now, we write the expression in terms of [MATH: \downarrow.] Using the definition of Peirce arrow, [MATH: \lnot \left(A \lor B \right) \equiv A \downarrow B,] followed by the fact that [MATH: \lnot A \equiv A \downarrow A,] we get
[MATH: ¬(¬x∨y)|≡¬x↓y; ≡(x↓x)↓y.]

Content:
Therefore, expressed using only [MATH: \downarrow,] we have
[MATH: x \land \lnot y \equiv (x \downarrow x) \downarrow y.]

---

Content:
Similarly, the set [MATH: \{\mid\}] (Sheffer stroke) is functionally complete. Here's the proof.

Content:
> Since [MATH: \{\lnot, \land\}] is a functionally complete set, any Boolean function can be expressed in terms of only [MATH: \lnot] and [MATH: \land.]
>
> In this expression, we can replace any occurrence of conjunction [MATH: \land] using the definition of Sheffer stroke:
> [MATH: A \mid B \equiv \lnot \left(A \land B \right)]
> Then, we can replace any occurrence of negation [MATH: \lnot] using the definition of the Sheffer stroke for two identical variables:
> [MATH: A∣A|≡¬(A∧A); ≡¬A]
> The resulting expression uses only [MATH: \mid.] Therefore, any Boolean function can be expressed in terms of [MATH: \mid,]; hence, the set [MATH: \{\mid\}] is functionally complete.

Content:

Second, we use the definition of Sheffer stroke [MATH: A \mid B \equiv \lnot \left(A \land B\right){:}]

[MATH: ¬¬(x∧y)≡¬(x∣y)]

Finally, recall that [MATH: \lnot A \equiv A \mid A{:}]

Item 14 — Tutorial: Minimal Functionally Complete Sets

Content:
A functionally complete set of Boolean functions is minimal if it has no functionally complete proper subset.
In other words, removing any single element results in a no longer functionally complete set.

Content:
For example, [MATH: \{\lnot, \land\}] is a minimal functionally complete set. If we remove [MATH: \land,] then the Boolean function [MATH: f \equiv x \land y] cannot be expressed using only [MATH: \lnot.]

Content:
On the other hand, [MATH: \{\lnot, \land, \lor\}] is not a minimal functionally complete set. It has proper subsets that are also functionally complete, namely [MATH: \{\lnot, \land\}] and [MATH: \{\lnot, \lor\}.]

Content:
